title: Trump's New Arc de Trump Renderings Looked Like Vanity With Federal Stationery
description_short: Trump's New Arc de Trump Renderings Looked Like Vanity With Federal Stationery
description_medium: The Trump administration released new renderings for a proposed 250-foot triumphal arch at Memorial Circle, near Arlington Memorial Bridge, the Guardian and Washington Post reported. The design included a 60-foot golden Lady Liberty and was intended to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary. Officials had begun seeking formal approval, while military veterans sued, arguing the structure would alter views of Arlington National Cemetery.
description_long:
On April 10, 2026, the Trump administration released renderings for a proposed 250-foot triumphal arch at Memorial Circle, at the foot of Arlington Memorial Bridge. The design by Harrison Design showed a 60-foot golden Lady Liberty figure and was intended to commemorate the United States’ 250th anniversary. The Washington Post reported that officials were beginning the formal approval process.

The proposal also faced a lawsuit from military veterans, who argued that the structure would alter important views of Arlington National Cemetery. The renderings made the scale and location of the project public, but they did not amount to final approval or establish that construction would go ahead. The linked reports describe a proposal entering review and a legal challenge to its effect on the memorial landscape. They do not provide a settled cost, funding plan or construction schedule. The dispute was therefore about the administration’s plan for a major new monument in a prominent public setting, with its design and visual impact contested before approval.

title: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie
description_short: Trump Promised Peace, but Dearborn Got Another Reminder of the Lie
description_medium: Associated Press reporters found Dearborn families waiting for news from relatives in Lebanon and mourning those already lost as the Iran conflict widened. Wayne County official Assad Turfe said he feared for an uncle and his family. The report set those anxieties against Trump’s promise of Middle East peace and the city’s large Arab American community.
description_long:
The Associated Press reported from Dearborn, Michigan, that families were waiting for news from relatives abroad and grieving people already lost as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran widened to Lebanon. Dearborn has one of the country’s largest Arab American communities, and many residents have family ties across the region. Wayne County official Assad Turfe told AP that he was waiting for word about an uncle, his wife, children and grandchildren in Lebanon.

The article contrasted those fears with Trump’s campaign promise to bring peace to the Middle East. It described a community where election-season protests had quieted, but conversations in mosques, at vigils and around family tables remained focused on loved ones’ safety. The report does not claim that every resident shared one political view; Turfe himself had been among the few Arab Americans to endorse Kamala Harris in 2024. Its account is a local portrait of how a regional conflict reached families in Dearborn through personal ties and uncertainty about relatives abroad.

title: Trump: Jared & Ivanka vacation in Croatia with Wendi Deng, meet with Russian oligarch
description_short: Trump: Jared & Ivanka vacation in Croatia with Wendi Deng, meet with Russian oligarch
description_medium: Ivanka Trump posted a photograph with Wendi Deng while vacationing in Croatia with Jared Kushner in August 2016. The linked TrumpFile account says Mueller-related records later described a meeting there between Donald Trump, Kushner, a Russian oligarch and the oligarch’s girlfriend, but it says the oligarch’s identity was not public. Claims about Deng and Vladimir Putin are presented as rumor.
description_long: The linked TrumpFile page says FOIA-obtained Mueller records described a meeting in Croatia between Donald Trump, Jared Kushner, a Russian oligarch and the oligarch’s girlfriend. It does not identify the oligarch or describe the meeting. The page also repeats rumors about Wendi Deng and Vladimir Putin and claims intelligence officials warned Kushner about Deng, without supplying the underlying records. The identity, corroborating documents and Mueller’s findings remain unclear.

title: Trump: The NRA spends $30 million to help elect Donald Trump through illegal coordination
description_short: Trump: The NRA spends $30 million to help elect Donald Trump through illegal coordination
description_medium: The NRA spent about $30 million supporting Trump’s 2016 campaign, according to the linked account. On October 19, 2016, the NRA and campaign bought ads on the same networks for matching dates and times. The account says Jon Ferrell authorized both sets of purchases through separate media firms; former FEC general counsel Larry Noble called the evidence strong, but no legal finding is cited.
description_long:
The linked account says the National Rifle Association spent about $30 million supporting Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign. On October 19, the NRA bought pro-Trump television advertising through Red Eagle Media. The Trump campaign separately purchased advertising on the same networks for the same dates and times through American Media & Advocacy Group.

The article says Jon Ferrell, a chief financial officer at National Media Research, Planning and Placement, authorized both sets of purchases. Former Federal Election Commission general counsel Larry Noble described the overlap as “very strong evidence, if not proof,” of illegal coordination. The account presents that as an expert’s assessment of the ad-buy pattern, not a court or FEC finding. The dates, networks and shared authorization raise a campaign-finance question about whether the purchases were coordinated, but the linked material does not report an adjudication establishing a violation. It is more accurate to describe the parallel purchases and the concern raised by the former FEC official than to state that a legal violation was conclusively proven.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: The NRA spends $30 million to help elect Donald Trump through illegal coordination

title: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him
description_short: Trump purges 46 attorneys from the DOJ, including one asked to investigate him
description_medium: Attorney General Jeff Sessions requested the resignations of 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Obama in March 2017. The TrumpFile account says ethics watchdogs had urged New York U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara to investigate possible Emoluments Clause violations, but it does not say a formal investigation had begun or link his departure to that matter. Officials said the mass resignations had been planned earlier.
description_long:
In March 2017, Attorney General Jeff Sessions asked 46 U.S. attorneys appointed under Barack Obama to resign. The linked account says officials maintained that the departures had been planned before the requests were made, while the mass, immediate nature of the resignations drew attention. Preet Bharara, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, was among the prosecutors who received a request to leave.

The source notes that government watchdogs had recently urged Bharara to investigate whether Trump had violated the Constitution’s Emoluments Clause by receiving payments from foreign governments. It does not say that a formal investigation had opened or that Bharara’s dismissal was ordered to stop one. Fox commentator Sean Hannity had called for Trump to “purge” Obama-era officials the day before the requests, but officials said the plan predated that broadcast. The episode documents the unusually broad turnover and its timing alongside calls for an inquiry; it does not establish that the inquiry caused Bharara’s departure.

title: Trump: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher meets with Julian Assange for a pardon quid pro quo
description_short: Trump: Rep. Dana Rohrabacher meets with Julian Assange for a pardon quid pro quo
description_medium: Representative Dana Rohrabacher met Julian Assange, activist Charles Johnson and Assange’s lawyer at the Ecuadorian Embassy in London in 2017. The linked account says Assange wanted an assurance against arrest in exchange for information about Russia’s role in the 2016 leaks, and Rohrabacher said he would raise an arrangement with the White House. It does not show Trump approved a pardon.
description_long:
Representative Dana Rohrabacher met Julian Assange, activist Charles Johnson and Assange’s lawyer at the Ecuadorian Embassy in London in August 2017. The linked account says Assange offered information that could support the claim that Russia was not responsible for the 2016 WikiLeaks disclosures, while seeking assurance that he would not be arrested if he left the embassy.

Rohrabacher later said he believed someone had extracted the emails and attributed the hack to Russia, and that he hoped the meeting could help establish that. The account quotes him promising to return to the White House and see whether an arrangement could be made. It describes a proposed exchange and a request for protection, not a pardon granted or an agreement authorized by Trump. The source does not show that the White House accepted the proposal or that Assange’s offer was verified. The meeting is documented in the linked account; the alleged quid pro quo and its ultimate outcome should remain attributed rather than treated as a completed deal.

title: Trump: McConnell and Rand Paul block sanctions on Kremlin company and Manafort business partner
description_short: Trump: McConnell and Rand Paul block sanctions on Kremlin company and Manafort business partner
description_medium: The Senate voted 57–42 on a measure to restore sanctions on Rusal, falling short of the 60 votes needed to advance it. Mitch McConnell opposed the effort, and Rand Paul also voted against it, the linked account reported. Rusal was associated with Oleg Deripaska, a business associate of Paul Manafort; the vote did not itself establish why the senators opposed the measure.
description_long:
On January 16, 2019, the Senate voted 57–42 on a measure to enforce sanctions against Rusal, a Russian aluminum company associated with Oleg Deripaska, a business associate of Paul Manafort. The effort fell three votes short of the 60-vote threshold required to advance. Eleven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure; Mitch McConnell campaigned against it, and Rand Paul opposed it.

The linked account says the House had earlier voted 362–53 to enforce the sanctions. It also cites a later Senate Intelligence Committee report describing Rusal as a tool in Vladimir Putin’s influence efforts. Those facts provide context for the company and the debate, but they do not establish that the senators’ votes were motivated by a relationship with Deripaska or Manafort. The immediate outcome was procedural: the Senate did not reach the threshold to advance the sanctions measure. The vote and its shortfall are distinct from subsequent investment plans involving Rusal and a Kentucky aluminum project.

title: Trump: Judge orders Donald Trump to pay $2m for illegal use of charity funds
description_short: Trump: Judge orders Donald Trump to pay $2m for illegal use of charity funds
description_medium: A New York court approved a settlement requiring Donald Trump to pay $2 million in a case over misuse of Trump Foundation funds. Trump made 19 admissions, including that the foundation paid for a portrait displayed at a Trump hotel, covered obligations of his businesses, and gave his campaign control of about $2.8 million raised at an Iowa veterans’ fundraiser.
description_long:
In November 2019, a New York judge approved a settlement in the state attorney general’s case over the Trump Foundation. Donald Trump agreed to pay $2 million and made 19 admissions concerning the charity’s use of funds. He acknowledged that the foundation bought a $10,000 portrait of him that was displayed at a Florida hotel, paid obligations of for-profit businesses including Mar-a-Lago and a Westchester golf club, and gave his presidential campaign control of about $2.8 million raised at an Iowa veterans’ fundraiser.

Trump acknowledged that the fundraiser was a campaign event. The settlement’s admissions described specific uses of charitable money for his businesses and campaign, while the $2 million payment was below the $8 million the attorney general had sought. The case had begun in June 2018. The court-approved agreement resolved the state proceeding on those terms; the payment and admissions are the documented outcome, rather than a separate criminal conviction.
